title: Benchmarks: published figures on young people, work and health-related benefits
note: Reference figures from the review (From a Welfare State to a Working State, 17 November 2026) and other sources, as published, each with its own definitions, coverage and date. Where PolicyEngine has a comparable figure, it is shown beside the published one with its build and year.

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training (NEET)
rows.basis: Labour Force Survey estimate, April to June 2026, UK: 13.0% of people aged 16 to 24. The review describes the number as nearly one million young people, 1 in 8
rows.source: Office for National Statistics

rows.figure: NEET rate the review projects for 2036-37 with its recommendations
rows.basis: Share of people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training, UK, from 13.1% in 2026-27: the review's internal modelling (data tables, table 3). The review's ambition is around 5% (paragraph 142)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: data tables

rows.figure: Young people on Universal Credit health with no work requirements
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation analysis
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 receiving the Universal Credit health element
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation response to the review: people aged 16 to 24 currently receiving the health element of Universal Credit
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Young people receiving incapacity benefits, as stated in the review
rows.basis: The review's own count (paragraph 633): more than double the number in 2012
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people receiving Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
rows.value: 450,000; worth around £8,400 a year on average
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation response to the review: young people currently receiving PIP
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: PIP recipients aged 18 to 24, UK; 16 and 17-year-olds are not counted
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2027-28 baseline caseload

rows.figure: Young people aged 16 to 24 receiving Disability Living Allowance or PIP, as stated in the review
rows.value: Over 400,000; 820,000 expected to receive PIP in ten years
rows.basis: The review's own count from DWP Stat-Xplore (paragraph 633): double the number in 2012. The projection is 1 in 9 young people in the UK
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people the review expects its recommendations to help into sustained work by 2036
rows.basis: Modelling carried out for the review: the whole set of recommendations, not the benefit changes alone
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Young people affected by the modelled package
rows.basis: No published figure: shown for the PolicyEngine estimate only

policyengine_estimate.label: People aged 16 to 24 in households made worse off by the combined package

rows.figure: Spending on PIP and Universal Credit health for young people
rows.basis: The review's figures for ages 16 to 24 (paragraph 114): PIP of £3.8bn and the Universal Credit LCWRA element of £0.92bn in 2025-26
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: Static saving in 2029-30 from removing the UC health element for under-25s and PIP for ages 18 to 24, UK: the Exchequer saving, including knock-on effects on other benefits (such as carer benefits and the UC housing element), so not the same as spending on PIP and the health element; PIP at 16 and 17 is not removed
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: PIP spending on people aged 16 to 24
rows.value: £3.8bn a year; £1.3bn in 2019-20, forecast at £8.1bn in 2036-37
rows.basis: The review's figure for 2025-26, ages 16 to 24 (footnote to paragraph 114)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: Static Exchequer saving from removing PIP for ages 16 to 24 in 2029-30, UK, including knock-on effects on other benefits (such as carer benefits and the UC housing element), so not the same as PIP spending; £3.64bn for ages 18 to 24
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: Universal Credit LCWRA element spending on people aged 16 to 24
rows.value: £0.92bn a year; £0.42bn in 2019-20, forecast at £0.68bn in 2036-37
rows.basis: The review's figure for 2025-26, ages 16 to 24 (footnote to paragraph 114)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

policyengine_estimate.basis: Static saving from removing the UC health element for under-25s in 2029-30, UK
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: Annual welfare saving the review estimates for 2036-37
rows.basis: PIP and Universal Credit spending, UK, in 2026-27 prices, against the baseline forecast: replacement awards for some claimants, the cost of a Youth Allowance and a work allowance, and an assumed employment effect. Savings begin in 2029-30
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

policyengine_estimate.basis: Static saving in 2029-30, UK: from the pre-report central variant (severe cases kept, PIP at half rate) to the report's package, full removal of the UC health element for under-25s and PIP for ages 18 to 24, with every existing claimant reached from April 2029
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: Cumulative welfare savings the review estimates by 2036-37
rows.basis: Sum of annual savings over the eight years from 2029-30 to 2036-37, UK, in 2026-27 prices (paragraph 113 and the analytical annex)
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State

rows.figure: Annual cost of the review's recommendations in 2036-37
rows.value: £5.8bn in 2036-37; a net saving of about £0.2bn after welfare savings and fiscal offsets
rows.basis: Gross cost in 2026-27 prices (data tables, table 2): education £2.1bn, Opportunity and Support Guarantees £1.9bn, youth hiring incentives £1.1bn, health £0.7bn; set against £3.6bn of welfare savings and £2.4bn of fiscal offsets
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: data tables

rows.figure: Cost of the review's youth hiring incentives in 2036-37
rows.basis: Gross cost in 2026-27 prices of expanding the Youth Jobs Grant by up to 40,000 places a year and of the apprenticeship recommendations. The annex gives no separate cost for the employer National Insurance change the review proposes
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

rows.figure: Incapacity benefit spending on people aged 18 to 24
rows.basis: IFS analysis
rows.source: Institute for Fiscal Studies

rows.figure: Cost of a zero employer National Insurance rate for under-25s
rows.value: £5.1bn a year; about £132,000 per extra job
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation estimate, based on 2026 data; not a recommendation of the review, which proposes a higher employer National Insurance threshold for workers aged 21 to 24 instead
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

policyengine_estimate.basis: Static cost of a zero employer National Insurance rate for under-25s in 2029-30, UK
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: Change in relative poverty after housing costs the review estimates
rows.basis: People in relative low income after housing costs once the modelled measures are fully rolled out, to the nearest 50,000: benefit changes with replacement awards, a Health and Disability Fund, a Youth Allowance, a work allowance and 440,000 more young people in work
rows.source: From a Welfare State to a Working State: analytical annex

policyengine_estimate.basis: People in relative poverty after housing costs in 2029-30, UK: static effect of removing the UC health element for under-25s and PIP for ages 18 to 24, with no replacement benefit and no one moving into work
policyengine_estimate.label: PolicyEngine, build fcfac709, 2029-30

rows.figure: Young people kept out of poverty by UC health and/or PIP
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation analysis
rows.source: Resolution Foundation

rows.figure: Young PIP claimants reporting no extra costs
rows.basis: Resolution Foundation research
rows.source: Resolution Foundation
